blk_part_01_part_1_frances_lunch_is_buil.text: Start with France. Many people picture the French lunch as long and slow, with wine and several courses. The real rules tell a more ordered story. In France, the legal full-time workweek is 35 hours, and work beyond that counts as overtime. A working day can last up to 10 hours. In special cases, such as a very busy period or the needs of how a company is organised, it can last up to 12 hours. So the 35-hour week does not simply mean short days. It sets a clear limit, and extra hours have a cost.

blk_part_01_part_1_frances_lunch_is_buil.text: Lunch fits inside this system. After six hours of work in a row, an employee must get a break of at least 20 minutes, and lunch counts as that break. In practice, lunch breaks are often longer, at around 45 minutes. That is real time to sit down and eat, but it is not the two-hour meal of the stereotype. Lunch is also usually unpaid. This is because employees are not under their employer's direction during the break. The time belongs to them, not to the company.

Companies with 50 or more employees must provide a room where staff can store food, heat it and sit down. Think about the message behind this rule. Eating is treated as something that deserves a proper space, not something you do quickly at your desk. This fits a wider French culture that values enjoying food. Still, the picture is not frozen. Fast food and American eating habits put pressure on French food culture, especially among young people. Many French people protect traditional food culture through education and laws.

blk_part_02_part_2_in_the_usa_the_meal_c.text: Car use is widespread in the United States, and it changed how people eat. It made drive-in and drive-through restaurants popular. At a drive-through, you order, pay and collect your food without leaving your seat. The mechanism is simple. When the car is at the center of daily movement, the meal has to come to the car. Food must be quick to serve and easy to eat on the move. This helps explain why American eating today puts a strong focus on fast food and take-out. Familiar examples include burgers, pizza, hot dogs, fried foods and milkshakes.

blk_part_03_part_3_japan_packed_the_meal.text: Farmers had their own version. They carried wooden bento boxes called menpa, filled with barley rice and pickled plums. This food stayed fresh even when it was cold, which mattered when there was nowhere to heat it. On long days such as rice planting, villagers shared large wooden buckets of rice balls and side dishes and ate together. Bentos also went to the theater. Makunouchi bentos, with grilled rice balls, fish cakes and simmered dishes, were served during breaks between acts. The style is still common today.

In the 20th century, the chef Escoffier codified modern haute cuisine, which means he set out its rules in an organised way. Yet the everyday start of the day can be very simple. blk_part_04_part_4_geography_shapes_the_.text: Each of these images hides a cause. The American meal follows the car across a huge country. The Japanese bento grew from longer working days and a need for food that travels well. These are also patterns, not rules.
